title: Job 29:11–25
context: Job explains why he was honored: he delivered the poor who cried and the fatherless who had no helper, made the widow’s heart sing, was eyes to the blind and feet to the lame, a father to the needy, and broke the power of the unrighteous (29:11–17). These claims stand in direct tension with Eliphaz’s earlier charges that Job had stripped the naked, withheld bread from the hungry, and sent widows away empty (22:5–9). This page does not harmonize the two accounts; the reader is left to weigh them against the narrator’s description of Job (1:1, 1:8) and the LORD’s later word about the three friends (42:7). Job then recalls his old expectation of dying in his own house, counting his days “as the sand” (29:18); the Hebrew word here is uncertain, and some translations render it with the name of a long-lived bird instead, so this page holds the image loosely. He closes by remembering how people waited for his counsel as for rain, and how he sat as chief, “as one who comforts the mourners” (29:21–25). Both traditions read the unit as Job’s sober account of his former integrity, offered as part of the path to his oath in chapter 31, not as self-praise to be rebuked.

verses.text: For when the ear heard me, then it blessed me, and when the eye saw me, it commended me,
verses.arminianNotes: Those who heard and saw Job blessed and commended him. Arminian readers note that Job is explaining the source of his honor. The people’s praise, he says, rested on how he treated others, which he describes in the next verses.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise read the verse as introducing the reason for Job’s esteem. Shared ground: both traditions read it as leading into his account of justice and mercy in 29:12–17, and both read that account alongside the narrator’s description of Job (1:1).

verses.text: because I delivered the poor who cried, and the fatherless also, who had no one to help him,
verses.arminianNotes: Job was honored “because I delivered the poor who cried, and the fatherless also.” Arminian readers note Job’s active care for the vulnerable. This claim stands in direct tension with Eliphaz’s charge that the arms of the fatherless were broken (22:9).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see Job’s care for the poor and fatherless as the righteousness God’s people are called to show. Shared ground: both traditions note the conflict with Eliphaz’s charges (22:5–9) and do not harmonize it, letting 1:1 and 42:7 inform the reader’s judgment.

verses.text: the blessing of him who was ready to perish came on me, and I caused the widow’s heart to sing for joy.
verses.arminianNotes: The blessing of the perishing came on Job, and he made the widow’s heart sing. Arminian readers note the contrast with Eliphaz’s claim that Job sent widows away empty (22:9). Job remembers widows rejoicing instead.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the joy of the widow as the fruit of practical mercy. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as Job’s testimony against the friends’ charges, without settling the matter by harmonizing the two accounts.

verses.text: I put on righteousness, and it clothed me. My justice was as a robe and a diadem.
verses.arminianNotes: “I put on righteousness, and it clothed me.” Arminian readers note the image of righteousness as clothing, worn openly and daily. Job claims that justice was not occasional for him but characteristic of how he lived.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the clothing image as describing a life marked by justice. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as Job’s claim to integrity, which the narrator supports (1:1), without reading it as a claim to sinlessness.

verses.text: I was eyes to the blind, and feet to the lame.
verses.arminianNotes: “I was eyes to the blind, and feet to the lame.” Arminian readers note the beautiful image of practical help. Job did not only give gifts from a distance but made up for what others lacked, serving them in their weakness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the image as a picture of mercy that meets real needs. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as describing the kind of compassion Scripture commends, and both see it as part of Job’s defense rather than boasting.

verses.text: I was a father to the needy. I researched the cause of him whom I didn’t know.
verses.arminianNotes: “I was a father to the needy. I researched the cause of him whom I didn’t know.” Arminian readers note Job’s diligence in justice. He took up the cases even of strangers, making sure they received a fair hearing.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a picture of impartial justice that seeks out the truth. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as part of Job’s portrait of righteous leadership, standing in tension with Eliphaz’s charges (22:5–9).

verses.text: I broke the jaws of the unrighteous and plucked the prey out of his teeth.
verses.arminianNotes: Job broke the jaws of the unrighteous and plucked the prey from his teeth. Arminian readers note the vivid image of rescuing victims from oppressors. Job’s care for the weak included confronting those who harmed them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see justice as including the restraint of evildoers. Shared ground: both traditions read the image as poetry of protection, not as literal violence, and both see it as completing Job’s account of his former righteousness.

verses.text: Then I said, ‘I will die in my own house, I will count my days as the sand.
verses.arminianNotes: Job expected to die in his own house and count his days “as the sand.” Arminian readers note that the Hebrew word rendered “sand” is uncertain, and some render it with the name of a long-lived bird. Either way, Job expected a long life.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hold the uncertain word loosely and do not build on it. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as Job’s former expectation of a long, settled life, an expectation his present suffering has overturned.

verses.text: My root is spread out to the waters. The dew lies all night on my branch.
verses.arminianNotes: “My root is spread out to the waters. The dew lies all night on my branch.” Arminian readers note the image of a well-watered tree. Job once felt secure and flourishing, nourished by blessing that seemed unending.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise read the tree as an image of prosperity, perhaps echoing other biblical pictures of the righteous as a planted tree. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as part of Job’s remembered confidence.

verses.text: My glory is fresh in me. My bow is renewed in my hand.’
verses.arminianNotes: “My glory is fresh in me. My bow is renewed in my hand.” Arminian readers note the images of vigor and strength. Job expected his honor and power to remain renewed, not to be lost as they now have been.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the images as completing Job’s former expectation of lasting strength. Shared ground: both traditions read 29:18–20 as Job’s memory of what he once assumed, setting up the reversal described in chapter 30.

verses.text: “Men listened to me, waited, and kept silence for my counsel.
verses.arminianNotes: People listened, waited, and kept silent for Job’s counsel. Arminian readers note that Job returns to the theme of his respected words. His counsel was once eagerly received, unlike his present experience with his friends.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the contrast with the friends, who have not heard Job’s words as he wished. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as remembrance of honor, and both see its painful contrast with Job’s present isolation.

verses.text: After my words they didn’t speak again. My speech fell on them.
verses.arminianNotes: After Job’s words, they did not speak again; his speech fell on them. Arminian readers note the image of words received as final and weighty. Job’s counsel once settled matters rather than provoking dispute.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise read the verse as describing the authority of wise counsel. Shared ground: both traditions read it as part of Job’s portrait of his former standing, without scolding him for remembering it.

verses.text: They waited for me as for the rain. Their mouths drank as with the spring rain.
verses.arminianNotes: They waited for Job as for the rain and drank his words as spring rain. Arminian readers note the image of refreshment. Job’s counsel brought life to others, much as rain brings life to dry ground.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the rain image as describing counsel that blesses and refreshes. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as poetry of remembered usefulness, which deepens the sorrow of Job’s present condition.

verses.text: I smiled on them when they had no confidence. They didn’t reject the light of my face.
verses.arminianNotes: Job smiled on those who had no confidence, and they did not reject the light of his face. Arminian readers note Job’s encouragement of the discouraged. His presence brought hope to those who lacked it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise read the verse as describing gracious leadership that lifts others up. The exact sense of the lines is debated, and both hold it loosely. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as part of Job’s memory of comforting others.

verses.text: I chose out their way, and sat as chief. I lived as a king in the army, as one who comforts the mourners.
verses.arminianNotes: Job sat as chief, “as one who comforts the mourners.” Arminian readers note the poignant ending. Job once comforted mourners, but now he is a mourner whose friends have failed to comfort him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the irony that the comforter now needs comfort. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as closing Job’s remembrance with a picture of compassionate leadership, preparing for the reversal of chapter 30.
